subject: moving-continents
title: The Puzzle of Moving Continents
summary: One scientist noticed the continents fit like puzzle pieces.

cards.title: Earth is a puzzle
cards.text: Look at a world map. The east side of South America and the west side of Africa look like they could fit together like puzzle pieces. Is that just luck?

cards.title: A wild idea
cards.text: In 1912, a German scientist named Alfred Wegener said the continents used to be one giant piece of land. He called it Pangaea, which means "all lands." Over a very long time, he said, the pieces drifted apart.

cards.title: Clues in the rocks
cards.text: Wegener found the same kinds of fossils on coasts of South America and Africa. Those plants and animals could not have swum across a huge ocean. Scientists had also found coal made from warm-weather plants in icy Antarctica.
cards.example: These clues made sense if the continents were once joined and in different places.

cards.title: Nobody believed him
cards.text: Most scientists said no. Wegener could not explain what force could push whole continents. He kept looking for proof until he died on an expedition in Greenland in 1930.

cards.title: Proof from the sea floor
cards.text: Years later, ships mapped the ocean floor. They found a long chain of underwater mountains and stripes in the rocks that matched on both sides. New sea floor was forming in the middle and spreading out. Wegener was mostly right!

cards.question: Wegener had good clues but no explanation for how continents move. Should scientists believe an idea before anyone can explain how it works?
nudges: What if a new idea turns out to be wrong?

options.text: A giant piece of land made of all the continents together

options.why: Pangaea was land. It broke apart, and oceans formed between the pieces.
Good guess, but Pangaea was a supercontinent.

questions.q: Why did most scientists not believe Wegener at first?

options.text: He could not explain what force moved the continents.
options.why: Right. Good clues were not enough without an explanation.

options.text: He had no clues at all.
options.why: He had clues: matching coastlines, fossils, and coal in Antarctica.

options.text: He was not a real scientist.
options.why: He was a scientist. The problem was the missing "how."

questions.q: Where did the strongest new proof come from?

options.why: Yes. Mountains and matching rock stripes showed new sea floor spreading out.
The proof came from Earth's ocean floor.
Not quite. Ships studying the ocean floor found the proof.

sources.title: Historical perspective (This Dynamic Earth)
sources.supports: Ortelius in 1596; Wegener's 1912 continental drift; matching coastlines and fossils; coal in Antarctica; the missing force; Wegener's death in 1930; the open question of what drives plates.

sources.title: Developing the theory (This Dynamic Earth)
sources.supports: Echo-sounding and the mid-ocean ridge (more than 50,000 km long); thin seafloor sediment found in 1947; zebra-like magnetic striping; seafloor spreading; the 1968 Glomar Challenger drill cores.
